title: How did you get the sound effects for your last game?
author: eyepia
selftext:
I’m building a game audio library, and I’m curious how people here put together the sound effects for their games. Did you mostly use asset packs, generate them with AI, or mix a few approaches?

I’d love to hear about one sound in particular. How did you make or find it, and why did you go that route?

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
[humblebundle.com](https://www.humblebundle.com) — I've been purchasing professional sample libraries for more than five years, and I've built up quite a collection.

I can now also create my own game music using ACE 1.5, trained around my own creative direction and production style.

For more sophisticated music production, I've taken things a step further and built my own AI producer that routes the entire AI music-production process through an actual DAW. I'm currently working with FL Studio and REAPER.

The AI handles the musical arrangement, VST instruments, samples, mixing, mastering, and final output. I can export individual stems, 24-bit WAV files, streaming-ready audio, FLAC, MP3, and pretty much any other format I need.

The interesting part is that I'm using essentially the same professional production tools and workflows found in high-end recording studios. The finished music is virtually indistinguishable from traditionally produced studio recordings. There are no Suno or ACE 1.5 audio fingerprints in the final production.

I'm also experimenting with LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), which allows me to fine-tune an existing AI model using a relatively small set of additional trained weights. In this case, I'm training it on my own extensive library of electronic music that I've composed and produced in FL Studio over the years.

The goal is to teach the model my own musical characteristics, arrangements, sounds, and production style, rather than simply generating generic AI music.

Essentially, I'm building an AI-assisted music production environment around my own music, my own sound libraries, and my own creative direction.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
I generate them with my own synthesizer in real time.

That synthesizer is NOT a game audio library, meaning it doesn't do mixing, panning, attenuation, limiting, doppler, muffling, reverb or anything a (3D) game audio library would do.

Neither does it do any kind of audio management, such as mapping abstract sound cues to actual sound effects, keeping track of audio sources as game objects, loading, caching, voice management, etc.

All it does is produce mono signals from parameters, which are then fed to the actual audio engine.

So this might give you at least two takeaways:
1. What a game audio engine does or should/could do (there's more than the things I listed, and I'm not an expert on this at all)
2. A game audio engine should allow sources other than static PCM data from files.

I wrote my own audio engine simply because I didn't like the licensing models of any of the alternatives (OpenAL, Wwise, etc.), and many of them come with too much bloat I don't need, such as asset workflows. The only foreign code I use is miniaudio, for the platform abstraction, which gives me an output device but nothing else.

With AI, rolling your own audio engine is no longer big deal. Learning audio engineering is the interesting part, and AI can be of great help here, as always.

The biggest architectural challenge was integrating it with the rest of the engine, particularly the ECS: What keeps track of sound emitters and the listener, their world space positiona and velocities, etc. None of the big commercial audio engines solve this, and they can't. On the contrary, using one that wasn't developed for your engine makes this problem worse, so you might be better off either rolling everything yourself or using a complete existing game engine that brings everything, including audio, like Unreal.

The main reason to choose an established audio engine like Wwise is probably that you can hire audio engineers who already know how to use it. Having to learn something new that you didn't build is already reason enough not to use anything exotic.

So don't get your hopes up that anyone will want to use your audio engine. If you want to build one for your own game, sure, go for it, you will probably be glad you did, but then you should build one that suits your own game's needs and fits into your own codebase, not something generic.

comments.author: NooneLikesYouBill
comments.body:
Fortunately I’ve always been a musician/audio nerd and years before I ever even thought about game dev I was doing both studio recording and live/foley work. Started as largely a means to an end for my own production work but the more I did it the more I really got into it.

I haven’t really done much with ai audio yet to be honest, the more traditional path is just so engrained in me at this point… but I’m really interested to see, when I start meeting with audio, if it will - for lack of a better way of saying it, make that part of my skill set redundant - and I can see the pov of all the anti ai people and why that scares them, but honestly that would be awesome! Gives me more room to try to tackle something new, or another subject I can get familiar with. The way I figure it, we all already know the kind of effort and determination goes into making a good game,hell just finishing a game.Ai making my work load just a little bit easier, I’m gonna complain? 😁

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body:
All the audio in the puzzle game I'm making right now came from ElevenLabs: 44 files, all sound effects except two music loops. One sound in particular is a character reaction: a courier who goes "ooh" when she notices the player.

Almost every effect prompt starts with the same block: "Dry close studio recording, isolated single event starting immediately, no background, no speech, no music, no reverberant tail." Then the sound itself. For the courier that was a young cheerful woman with a bright warm alto voice doing one bright little ooh, plus "exactly one brief nonverbal human vocalization, no intelligible words".

Her first take was too long for its slot in the game. Squeezing it in would have meant speeding it up nearly twice, so I generated a shorter take instead. The one I kept only needed about 5% speed-up and ends up at 0.62 s.

After that most effects get the same cleanup: a 25 Hz high-pass, the silence trimmed at both ends, a 0.5 ms fade in and a 12 ms fade out. Variants of the same sound are matched within 2 LU of each other so they don't jump in volume when the game picks one at random.

Why that route: I already pay for ElevenLabs, so it's my default, and the game needed wordless reactions in three specific character voices.
